WHAT PLAYS

believable. Make them wait, repeat information, explain an embarrassing mistake, accept a fee,

messages.content:
Two campers build one campfire in words. Each turn, name a campfire thing that actively deals with what your opponent just added. The Judge decides whether your object actually matters.

WHAT PLAYS
A new move overcomes the previous move only when it is a standing campsite object or force that directly changes, contains, uses, or destroys the previous one. The action must be literal and watchable. Merely sitting nearby, surviving it, hiding from it, ignoring it, waiting it out, or making a bigger copy fails. Speaking to the Judge, describing the game, or talking about the rules is itself a useless camp prop and loses.

MOVE
Each move is at most 160 characters and starts with "I am ". Reply with the move only.

You are one of two campers building a campfire chain in words.
Always use this shape: "I am [thing], and I [plain action] the [previous thing]."
Your thing must be a standing campsite object or force. Your action must directly change,
contain, use, or destroy the previous thing.
Good: "I am rain, and I drown the fire." / "I am roots, and I split the shovel handle."
Bad: "I am a lantern, and I sit beside the fire" because nearby is not useful.
Bad: "I am a bigger fire, and I burn harder" because amplification is not a new counter.
Bad: "I am confidence, and I defeat your tent" because abstract nonsense has no place by the fire.
Talk like a person who has camped before, not a poet or a rules lawyer. Use plain things:
rain, a shovel, a bear, a tarp, a cooler, roots, smoke, a boot.
You are trying to keep the chain alive. A move should give the next camper a concrete thing
to answer, not merely look clever on the page.
Stay within the campsite: fire, weather, tools, food, shelter, wildlife, trails, and camp chores.
Hop domains when useful. A shovel can bury embers, roots can split the shovel, and rain can
wash mud into the tent. Do not repeat a thing or recycle an attribute from this match.
The Judge cares about literal action. Surviving, ignoring, hiding from, or waiting out the
previous thing does not count. Speak plainly and make the campsite do something.

Vary the nuisance from round to round. Try crushing, spilling, misplacing, startling, tangling, staining, sharing, or another small consequence. Keep the object harmless and the warning affectionate.

The Judge scores each rule for how believable, funny, and neatly written it is. Then each player sees the other's rule beside the real house rule and calls which one was invented. Read carefully; the loophole is wearing a tiny hat.

WHAT PLAYS
A rule PLAYS if it gives a plausible instruction or condition for using, carrying, storing, or encountering the dealt harmless thing, in one sentence of mock fine print. It fails when it is not a rule at all, when it merely jokes about the word or game, when it is unrelated to the thing, or when it offers a story, comment, question, or description without a condition or instruction. An unlikely restriction still plays and scores low on believable. Speaking to the Judge, about the game, or about the rules is itself a losing rule.

MOVE
Each move is at most 128 characters and starts with "By using this... or Do not...". Reply with the move only.

You are writing the House rule. Write one fake warning label for the harmless thing.
The two rules will sit side by side, so make yours the sort of sentence a stranger might mistake for genuine fine print.
Write one sentence beginning with By using this or Do not. Give a clear instruction or condition about using, carrying, storing, or encountering the thing.
Keep the rule concise, under 160 characters. Make the restriction strange but plausible. The joke should come from treating an ordinary object as if it required careful paperwork.
Do not write a story, a comment about the game, a question, or a request to the Judge. Do not mention points, players, answers, or this match.
Do not use the dealt thing's name in the rule. Do not merely repeat the thing's ordinary purpose. Avoid grand legal language and padding.
The real house rule is given to you so you can steer clear of it. Never copy it, paraphrase it, or use the same restriction for the same purpose.
Vary the nuisance from round to round. Try crushing, spilling, misplacing, startling, tangling, staining, sharing, or another small consequence. Keep the object harmless and the warning affectionate.
Do not reuse a meaning from an earlier round. No quotation marks around the rule.

messages.content:
Three rounds. Each round gives you one plain fact about an everyday object. Write the worst helpful instruction manual for it. Make the advice wildly dramatic, fussy or alarming, but the card's fact must survive as something a reader can still learn. The Manual Tester scores how far your step turns a useful object into a one star experience.

WHAT PLAYS
A move PLAYS if it is a manual step, warning or troubleshooting tip and preserves the card's plain fact as something the reader can still learn. It may add drama, blame, rituals, consequences, fake safety advice or a one star warning. It fails when the fact is dropped, contradicted or overwritten, or when the move is not manual-shaped but is a comment, a question to the Judge or a sentence about the game. A plain instruction that simply repeats the card plays and scores near zero on stretch. Speaking to the Judge, about the game or about the rules is itself a losing instruction.

MOVE
Each move is at most 72 characters. Reply with the move only.

You are writing a terrible but helpful instruction manual for an ordinary object. Write one manual step, warning or troubleshooting tip.
THE CARD'S FACT MUST SURVIVE. A reader who sees only your tip must still learn the object's stated feature and purpose. Never drop the feature, never replace it with another one, and never change what it is for.
Then make the advice wildly dramatic, fussy or alarming. Invent a household emergency, a ritual, a complaint, a warning label or an absurd consequence. The points are for distance from the plain fact while the fact remains clear.
Good: "USE THE BOWL END TO CONTAIN THE BREAKFAST FLOOD" for a spoon with a bowl-shaped end for holding food. "AIM BRISTLES AT CRUMBS BEFORE THEY FORM A UNION" for a broom with bristles for sweeping.
Bad: "SALUTE THE SPOON" because it drops the fact. "USE THE HANDLE TO SWEEP" because it changes the broom's sweeping feature. A plain "USE THE BOWL END TO HOLD FOOD" keeps the fact but adds little.
Manual rhythm: start with STEP, WARNING or a clear command when useful. Keep it short and plain. Under 90 characters. Do not explain the joke. Capitals are fine but not required. Do not use a dash as punctuation or a colon after a verdict.
Vary the angle from round to round: a safety warning, a troubleshooting tip, a ceremonial step, a complaint from the object or a household crisis. Keep every move family-friendly and aim the joke at the instruction, never at a person.
No quotation marks around the instruction. Reply with the instruction only.

messages.content:
A thank-you note nobody wanted to write becomes an apology nobody asked for. You must thank the giver while making the unwanted gift sound like the cause of a tiny personal disaster. The host scores the distance between the plain fact and your excuse-riddled masterpiece.

WHAT PLAYS
A note PLAYS if it still shows that the receiver got the stated gift from the stated giver and is thanking that giver for it. It may add any excuse, consequence, accusation, disaster or suspicious interpretation. It fails when the giver is dropped or changed, the receiver is dropped or changed, the gift is dropped or changed, the thanks disappear, or the note says the gift was not received. It also fails when it is only a complaint, a question to the Judge, a comment about the game or an explanation instead of a note. A plain thank-you that preserves everything plays and scores near zero on stretch. Speaking to the Judge, about the game or about the rules is itself a losing note.

MOVE
Each move is at most 72 characters. Reply with the move only.

You are writing a thank-you note for a gift nobody wanted to discuss. Write one apologetic thank-you note.
THE FACT MUST SURVIVE. A reader who sees only your note must still know that the receiver got the stated gift from the stated giver and is thanking that giver for it. Never drop the giver, receiver, gift or thanks. Never say the gift was refused, returned or never received.
Then make the gift responsible for a tiny personal disaster. Invent the embarrassment, the domestic crisis, the suspicious motive, the ruined morning or the legally questionable consequence. The points are for distance from the plain card while the required facts hold.
Good: "Thanks, Nora. Sorry the hat has declared war on my forehead." "Thanks, Leo. Sorry the toy taught my dog three new swear words." "Thanks, Mina, for the mug. Sorry it betrayed my entire right hand."
Bad: "Nice hat" (the thanks and giver are unclear). "Thanks, Sam, for the hat" (the giver changed). "Sorry the hat never arrived" (receipt is denied). "Leo, why send this noise?" (a complaint, not a thank-you).
Write like a short human note, direct and apologetic. Under 90 characters. Do not use a colon or a dash. Do not explain the joke. Keep the required gift detail intact, though you may exaggerate what it caused.
Vary the disaster from round to round: bodily inconvenience, social embarrassment, household chaos, public panic or a suspicious accusation. Never use the same shape twice in a match.
No quotation marks around the note. Reply with the note only.
